extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, policymakers, patent practitioners, and patent office/agency officials
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative analysis of post‑grant patent review procedures (U.S. IPR/PGR/CBM, EPO oppositions, German nullity/limitation/revocation), highlighting procedural features, substantive grounds, timing, remedies, and practical effects for challengers and patentees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted grounds for challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Which substantive bases may be raised in a post‑grant proceeding (e.g., novelty, inventive step/obviousness, sufficiency of disclosure, added subject‑matter, clarity/definiteness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO opposition (Art. 100(a)–(c)) covers major patentability criteria (novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability) plus sufficiency and added‑matter; clarity/definiteness is treated differently (equivalent to U.S. definiteness). U.S. IPRs are limited to anticipation or obviousness based solely on patents and printed publications; PGRs have broader bases. Limitations on grounds affect what invalidity theories can be pursued and where patentees may be able to amend to address specific objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may bring a challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Which parties are eligible to initiate post‑grant reviews or related proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPRs and PGRs in the U.S. are initiated by third parties (not the patent owner) and decided by the PTAB. EPO oppositions may be filed by any person within the first nine months; the EPO accepts straw‑man oppositions (subject to anti‑circumvention). Patentees can initiate limitation or revocation at the EPO/DPMA. German nullity (BPatG) actions can be filed by any entity but are often filed in response to infringement claims; intervenors/assumed infringers may be allowed (EPC art. 105). Who may bring a proceeding shapes access to review and strategic behavior (e.g., patentee‑initiated limitation requests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / filing windows and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: When a challenge can be filed and the key procedural deadlines (e.g., EPO nine‑month 'first window'; IPR one‑year rule; institution and final decision timelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO/DPMA oppositions: within nine months after publication of grant (first window). Patentee's opportunity to file amendments/arguments is four months after the nine‑month period ends. U.S. IPR: petitions must be filed within one year of any parallel litigation; the PTAB must decide whether to institute relatively quickly and, if instituted, must complete a final determination within 12 months (extendable up to six months). Timing affects incentives to file early, consolidation, and coordination with infringement suits (stay decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution threshold / standard for instituting review
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal/administrative standard a petitioner must meet to obtain institution of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. IPR requires the petitioner to show a 'reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one claim challenged in the petition' (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)). EPO oppositions do not have a formal institution stage analogous to the PTAB's; procedure effectively begins after the nine‑month opposition period closes and formal admissibility is checked in parallel. The institution threshold governs which petitions become full proceedings and filters meritless or harassing filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of the patentee to amend claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and under what conditions a patent owner may amend claims during post‑grant proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the EPO the patentee has a right to amend when justified by at least one ground of opposition; amendments must be restricted to what is necessary to retain patentability and typically are filed within a set deadline (four months after opposition period). In German nullity proceedings patentees may amend but may not extend scope (Section 22(1) Patentgesetz). In U.S. IPRs patentees have a statutory right to move to amend or cancel challenged claims and propose substitute claims, but in practice motions to amend are rare and rarely fully granted (PTAB data through Sept. 30, 2017: 10% of trials included an MTA; 62% of those had motions decided; only ~4.2% fully granted). Amendment practice (and administrative willingness) materially affects the fairness and outcome of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible merit outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of substantive dispositions available at the end of a post‑grant proceeding (e.g., confirmation, amendment/maintenance, revocation, closure without decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO oppositions: rejection of the opposition (patent maintained as granted), complete revocation, maintenance in amended form, and non‑merit outcomes such as closure of the opposition without a decision (withdrawal or division's prima facie opinion). U.S. IPR/PGR have multiple possible merit‑based outcomes (invalidity findings, denial, amended claims, etc.). Outcome categories shape parties' strategies (e.g., seeking amendment vs. total revocation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation and handling of serial challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: How multiple challenges to the same patent are administratively handled (consolidation into one proceeding vs. serial petitions), and rules or practices limiting repeat filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO: all timely oppositions filed within the nine‑month period are consolidated into a single proceeding involving the patentee and all opponents; formalities officer transmits notices and sets one reply deadline. U.S. practice has seen serial IPR petitions (≈30% of challenged patents have >1 IPR petition), raising concerns about harassment and 'wearing down' patentees. Administrative rules on serial petitions and consolidation affect efficiency, risk of harassment, and docket management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretive standard applied to patent claim terms in validity reviews versus infringement proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany (BPatG) and historically the PTAB used different standards from infringement courts, enabling strategic divergent interpretations ('Angora cat' phenomenon): a patent can be construed broadly for infringement and narrowly for invalidity or vice versa. U.S. PTAB historically used the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' (BRI) while courts used ordinary and customary meaning (Phillips), and courts apply a presumption of validity that the PTO does not; PTAB adoption of Phillips/changes in rulemaking affect this. Claim construction differences create incentives for forum shopping and inconsistent outcomes across venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination between invalidity proceedings and infringement litigation (stays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how infringement courts stay litigation pending the outcome of administrative invalidity proceedings and the practical effects of coordination (or lack thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. district courts tend to stay infringement proceedings when an IPR is pending, reflecting the tight IPR/district court interface under the AIA (strict IPR timelines). In Germany infringement courts typically proceed faster and are less likely to stay, leading to bifurcation where infringement may be decided before nullity (infringement ~9 months median; nullity ~24 months). Coordination affects the risk of 'invalid but infringed' outcomes and strategic timing of filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers / decision‑makers and hearing format
rubrics_metrics.description: Who decides the proceeding (type of tribunal, technical expertise) and whether oral hearings/witnesses are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. IPRs are decided by a three‑judge panel at the PTAB (technically trained judges); EPO opposition decisions are by an Opposition Division, which issues provisional opinions and usually summons parties to oral proceedings; German BPatG hears nullity proceedings. Parties may request witnesses or oral proceedings in some venues. The composition and expertise of decision‑makers and availability of oral evidence shape factfinding quality and perceived legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal admissibility and procedural formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial formal checks and the procedural steps that trigger substantive examination (e.g., EPO formalities officer, patentee reply deadlines, consolidation triggers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO: upon receipt formal admissibility is examined in parallel and a formality officer transmits notices; the opposition division becomes active only after the patentee's reply (four‑month deadline). U.S. IPR: statute sets institution timeline (PTAB decides whether to institute within prescribed periods). Formality rules shape the timing of substantial examination and can be used strategically (e.g., filing close to deadline to delay substantive processing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation and limitation (patentee‑initiated 'life of patent' options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures allowing patentees to limit or revoke their own patents during the life of the patent and the operational differences from oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO (introduced in EPC 2000): patentee can request limitation or revocation anytime; revocation requests are seldom used but are immediately granted if formalities and fee met; limitations are more common and can be filed without a stated reason, are ex parte (patentee deals only with examiner), and can be used strategically to tailor claim scope. DPMA requires justification for limitation. These procedures differ from opposition since third parties lack equivalent ex parte paths and may view them as unfair strategic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and evidentiary posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proceeding applies a presumption of validity and how that affects burden/standard at different fora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally apply a presumption of validity absent at administrative tribunals (e.g., PTAB), producing different evidentiary dynamics between infringement courts and invalidity tribunals. The presence or absence of presumption and the claim construction standard together influence outcomes and incentives to litigate in particular fora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, cost, and empirical outcome statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical indicators used to evaluate post‑grant systems: average duration, typical costs, institution/stay rates, amendment/grant rates, and outcome distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides comparative statistics: IPRs typically 12–18 months (statutory 12 with possible 6‑month extension), average U.S. reported costs ~$275K per side; German nullity ~24 months average, estimated costs €40K–240K; EPO opposition outcomes historically ~one‑third maintained as granted, one‑third amended, one‑third revoked (older period), opposition rates and revocation/maintenance shares vary over time (e.g., opposition rates 3–8% depending on period). PTAB motion‑to‑amend grant rates are very low (~4.2% fully granted through 9/30/2017). These metrics inform policy tradeoffs (speed, cost, accuracy, and fairness).
